# Extension — Study 09 (Phantom-Kernel): does a jump-robust vol rescue the "production fix"?

*The beat-7 worked complement. Generated by [`examples/extension.py`](../examples/extension.py)
on the seed-fixed simulator. Seed 0; fingerprint **`e9e85cbedf98`**.*

| Axis | Stamp | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **The rolling-vol "production fix", made jump-robust** | ![Not rescued](https://img.shields.io/badge/Not--rescued-8b949e?style=flat-square) | Bipower variation **mitigates** the collapse (World-B Sharpe **0.147 → 0.225**, ~2× the fills) but stays a fraction of plain fixed-σ AS (**1.503**). Removing jumps from the estimate isn't enough: in a stochastic-vol regime the *robust* vol still rises and widens the spread, so the book still under-trades. **Adapting spread width is the wrong lever — not just jump contamination.** |

## What the base study found
The article's first recommended adaptation is to feed a **rolling realised volatility** into the
AS spread. In the jumpy World B that fix **collapses**: naive realised variance `Σ rᵢ²` inhales
the jump variance, one jump spikes `σ̂`, the spread blows out, and almost nothing fills
(Sharpe **1.503 → 0.147**). See [`docs/results.md`](results.md).

## The repair under test
Replace the naive estimator with **bipower variation** (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard 2004),

    BV = (π/2) · mean(|rᵢ| · |rᵢ₋₁|),

which estimates the *diffusive* variance: a lone jump enters only ~two terms and is dominated,
so `σ̂` tracks the genuine volatility regime without spiking on a jump
([`JumpRobustASQuoter`](../phantom_kernel/strategies.py)). Three AS variants — fixed σ, naive
rolling vol, jump-robust rolling vol — face the **identical** order flow.

## World B (jumps + stochastic vol + informed flow) — where the fix was needed
```
                     terminal_pnl  pnl_sharpe  ci_lo  ci_hi  inv_std    n_fills
AS (fixed sigma)      13,525.8900      1.5030 1.3220 1.8360   0.6000 4,964.0000
AS (naive RV)            214.3400      0.1470 0.0790 0.2310   0.0500    76.0000
AS (jump-robust BV)      504.3000      0.2250 0.1630 0.3430   0.0900   175.0000
```

Jump-robustness **helps** — it roughly doubles the collapsed Sharpe and the fill count — but the
patient is still on the floor: **0.225** vs fixed-σ's **1.503**. The reason is structural:
World B also has *genuine* stochastic volatility, and bipower variation faithfully tracks it, so
in high-vol stretches the spread still widens and the book still under-fills. The damage was
never only jump contamination — it is that **adapting the spread width at all** sacrifices the
spread capture that fixed-σ AS keeps harvesting while the (k-free) inventory skew does the real
work.

## World A (calm, no jumps) — the control
```
                     terminal_pnl  pnl_sharpe  ci_lo  ci_hi  inv_std    n_fills
AS (fixed sigma)      13,909.9100      1.6350 1.4170 1.9590   0.6500 8,732.0000
AS (naive RV)         13,768.5900      1.5970 1.3870 1.9090   0.6600 8,658.0000
AS (jump-robust BV)   13,740.9600      1.5790 1.3740 1.8840   0.6600 8,644.0000
```

With no jumps the estimator choice is a **no-op**: all three AS variants land in the same place.
The jump-robust machinery costs nothing when there's nothing to be robust to — it simply fails
to add the value the fix was hoping for.

seed0            1.5030         0.1470               0.2250
seed1            1.4500         0.1200               0.1660

## Read
The article frames rolling realised vol as a clean upgrade; jump-robustness is the textbook way
to make it behave. It **isn't enough** — the fix is mitigated, not rescued. This *sharpens* the
study's core verdict rather than overturning it: the value in Avellaneda-Stoikov is the
**k-free inventory skew**, and every attempt to make the **spread-width** machinery smart (a
data-driven `k`, a rolling σ, now a jump-robust rolling σ) either misprices it or trades away
the edge. Keep the skew; quote the width with a fixed, sensible heuristic.
